name: Familial melanoma
aliases: familial atypical multiple mole melanoma syndrome

reference.source: DeVita, Hellman and Rosenberg's Cancer / NCCN genetic/familial guidelines
clinicalPearls: Most commonly caused by germline pathogenic variants in the CDKN2A tumour-suppressor gene, inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern with penetrance modified by ultraviolet exposure and skin type
Characterised by multiple primary cutaneous melanomas, often at young ages, and frequently many atypical (dysplastic) naevi
CDKN2A carriers also have an increased risk of pancreatic cancer, and some families show clustering of both melanoma and pancreatic malignancy
The gene encodes two proteins from alternative reading frames, p16INK4a and p14ARF, linking it to both the retinoblastoma and p53 tumour-suppressor pathways
Suspect the syndrome with multiple primary melanomas in one person or several affected close relatives, especially with early onset
Management emphasises rigorous sun protection, regular total-body skin surveillance with dermoscopy, and patient self-examination
Pancreatic surveillance is considered in CDKN2A families, particularly where pancreatic cancer has occurred
reference.pathophysiology: The syndrome usually results from a germline loss-of-function variant in CDKN2A, which encodes two distinct tumour suppressors through alternative reading frames. p16INK4a inhibits cyclin-dependent kinases 4 and 6 to hold cells in G1 via the retinoblastoma pathway, while p14ARF stabilises p53 by inhibiting its degradation. Loss of these functions removes key restraints on cell-cycle progression and on the apoptotic response to genomic stress, and when combined with ultraviolet-induced DNA damage in melanocytes this permits the accumulation of mutations that drive melanoma and contributes to pancreatic carcinogenesis.
additionalDifferentials: Sporadic melanoma in a person with heavy sun exposure
additionalInvestigations: Germline CDKN2A sequencing and deletion/duplication analysis, with CDK4 and multigene panel testing as appropriate
Regular total-body skin examination with dermoscopy and baseline photography
Biopsy and histopathology of suspicious pigmented lesions
Structured patient education in skin self-examination
Consideration of pancreatic imaging surveillance in CDKN2A families
Ophthalmological review where uveal involvement or BAP1-related disease is suspected
redFlags: A changing, irregular or bleeding pigmented lesion
A new melanoma in someone with prior primary disease
Painless jaundice, weight loss or new-onset diabetes suggesting pancreatic cancer
Rapidly enlarging or symptomatic lymph nodes indicating metastatic melanoma
reference.prognosis: Melanoma risk is high and lifelong, but early detection through surveillance and prompt excision yields excellent outcomes for thin lesions. Pancreatic cancer, when it occurs, carries a poorer prognosis, underscoring the value of risk reduction and, in selected families, pancreatic surveillance.
pitfalls: Attributing multiple melanomas to sun exposure alone and not considering a germline cause
Under-recognising the associated pancreatic cancer risk in CDKN2A carriers
Relying on infrequent examination when frequent dermoscopic surveillance detects earlier lesions
Failing to reinforce sun protection, which strongly modifies penetrance, and to offer cascade testing
references: DeVita, Hellman and Rosenberg's Cancer: Principles and Practice of Oncology
NCCN Guidelines: Genetic/Familial High-Risk Assessment and Melanoma
management: Enforce rigorous photoprotection with sun avoidance, protective clothing and broad-spectrum sunscreen to reduce ultraviolet-driven melanoma risk
Undertake regular total-body skin surveillance with dermoscopy and sequential photography, supported by structured skin self-examination
Perform prompt excisional biopsy of suspicious or changing pigmented lesions, with wide local excision for confirmed melanoma
Treat advanced disease via oncology with immune checkpoint inhibitors, or BRAF and MEK-targeted therapy where the tumour is BRAF-mutated
Offer pancreatic cancer surveillance imaging in CDKN2A families at additional risk, and counsel smoking cessation
Undertake germline CDKN2A testing, with CDK4 and multigene panel analysis as appropriate, alongside genetic counselling and cascade screening of relatives
Arrange ophthalmological review where uveal or BAP1-related disease is suspected
